Rabbi David HaLevi Segal: The Turei Zahav in the Mirror of the Generations
This article surveys the life and Torah contribution of Rabbi David HaLevi Segal, known by his appellation the Taz, who became one of the pillars of Ashkenazi halakhic decision-making in the 17th century. The text details the formative stages in the shaping of his personality, from his studies with his brother through his deep bond with his father-in-law, the Bach, highlighting his monumental work "Turei Zahav", which sought to restore clarity to halakha in an era of proliferating disputes. Beyond an analysis of his scholarly methodology, which combines intellectual toil with spiritual inspiration, the source describes his courageous leadership in the face of the decrees of Tach ve-Tat and the Sabbatean crisis, and illustrates how his innovative rulings have retained decisive authority throughout the generations. This survey seeks to present him not only as a brilliant legal commentator but as a spiritual shepherd who shaped the Jewish way of life out of destruction and revival.
The Work and Torah Teaching of Rabbi David HaLevi Segal: The Turei Zahav in the Mirror of the Generations
The history of Jewish law in the 17th century stands under the sign of codification and profound commentary, which shaped the Jewish way of life to this day. At the center of this period stands the towering figure of Rabbi David HaLevi Segal, known to every student of Torah by his appellation "the Taz", after his monumental work "Turei Zahav".[1, 2] The work of the Taz is not limited to the writing of a mere halakhic commentary; it represents the peak of Polish-Ashkenazi scholarship, which combined scholarly acuity, total commitment to the tradition of the "Tur", and a courageous confrontation with the upheavals of the age, from the decrees of Tach ve-Tat (5408–5409) to the Sabbatean crisis.[3, 4, 5] His Torah teaching, interwoven with intellectual toil and with elements of spiritual inspiration, became one of the pillars of the "Shulchan Arukh", and his authority as a decisor of the first rank has remained firm for hundreds of years.[4, 6, 7]
Roots and Growth: The Shaping of the Personality of a Halakhic Giant
Rabbi David HaLevi Segal was born in the year 5346 (1586) in the city of Ludmir (Volodymyr-Volynskyi) in the province of Volhynia, then part of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.[1, 3, 5] He grew up within a scholarly aristocracy; his father, Rabbi Shmuel HaLevi Segal, was a Torah scholar and exceedingly wealthy, who combined Torah and greatness at his table and was held in high esteem in his community.[3, 7] The lineage of the Taz reaches back to Rabbi Yitzchak Betzalel, one of the well-known sages of Poland, and his family was steeped in a tradition of spiritual and public leadership.[7, 8]
The Taz's early Torah education took place under the devoted guidance of his older brother, Rabbi Yitzchak HaLevi Segal, author of the responsa "Mahari HaLevi" and of the grammar books "Siach Yitzchak" and "Brit HaLevi".[1, 7, 8] The bond between the two brothers was especially deep, as the elder brother recognized the potential latent in young David and nurtured him as a prodigy.[7] Rabbi Yitzchak's influence on his brother is evident not only in his vast mastery of the Talmud but also in his meticulous attitude to language and linguistic precision, qualities that would later characterize the writing of the Taz.[7]
The Bond with the Bach: The Formative Years in the Home of Rabbi Yoel Sirkis
The most formative event of the Taz's youth was his marriage to Rebbetzin Rivka, daughter of Rabbi Yoel Sirkis, called "the Bach" after his work "Bayit Chadash".[1, 5, 9] The Bach was one of the greatest decisors of his generation, and his halakhic outlook, which sought to return to the sources of the law and to engage directly with the positions of the Rishonim and the Tur, deeply influenced his son-in-law. The Taz was supported at his father-in-law's table in Brisk and later in Krakow, a period in which he devoted himself to intensive study that shaped his methodology of halakhic analysis.[1, 4, 7]
Tradition preserves many stories about this period that emphasize the Taz's exceptional modesty. According to legend, at first the Bach did not recognize the greatness of his son-in-law's Torah learning, while the Taz for his part used to conceal his acuity in order to study undisturbed.[10] Only after an incident in which the Taz secretly placed the solution to a complicated difficulty on his father-in-law's table was his greatness revealed, and the Bach began to regard him as a disciple-colleague and as the continuer of his path.[10] The Taz's esteem for his father-in-law was so great that he quotes him hundreds of times in his work and calls him "my teacher and father-in-law" with the reverence reserved for one's principal teacher.[4, 5]
Wanderings and Rabbinate: From Communal Leadership to Literary Creation
After the years of study in his father-in-law's home, the Taz began a rabbinic career that led him among various communities in Poland.[1, 5] From the age of 23 he served in rabbinic posts, first in small communities such as Pultusk, and afterwards in more central cities such as Brisk and Krakow.[5, 6, 8] The period of his first rabbinate was often marked by poverty and severe financial hardship, in contrast to the wealth in which he had grown up in his father's home.[1, 7] His wanderings among seven different rabbinic posts sometimes stemmed from political or economic circumstances, but wherever he stayed he left an indelible Torah imprint.[1]
The Krakow Period and the Family Tragedy
During his tenure as rabbi in Krakow, the Taz suffered a severe personal tragedy when two of his children died.[1, 5] The Taz, with his tendency to see the hand of Providence in everything, attributed their deaths to the fact that he lived in an apartment allotted to him by the community above the synagogue building.[1, 8] Although from a strictly halakhic standpoint there is no absolute prohibition against living above a synagogue (under certain conditions), the Taz held that profane uses taking place above a holy place constitute an affront to the honor of the Divine Presence, and this approach found tangible expression in his work on the laws of prayer.[8]
The Flourishing in Ostroh and the Completion of the "Turei Zahav"
In the year 5401 (1641) the Taz was invited to serve as rabbi in the city of Ostroh (Ostra) in Volhynia, which at that time was a city full of sages and scribes and one of the most important spiritual centers in Eastern Europe.[1, 5, 7] In Ostroh the Taz found the tranquility required for great creative work; the heads of the community supported him financially and encouraged him to publish his works.[1, 7] There he founded a great yeshiva that drew hundreds of students, among them key figures of the next generation.[5, 7] In Ostroh the Taz completed the writing of the "Yoreh De'ah" part of his work, which was published in Lublin in the year 5406 (1646), and with this began the period of his worldwide renown as the decisor of the generation.[1, 5]
The Decrees of Tach ve-Tat: Destruction and Revival
The Taz's life in Ostroh was cruelly cut short with the outbreak of the Cossack uprising under the leadership of Bohdan Chmielnicki in 1648, known in Jewish history as the decrees of Tach ve-Tat.[4, 11] The Ostroh community, like many others in Ukraine and Poland, faced total destruction. The Taz was forced to flee for his life together with his family, managing to save the precious manuscripts of his works but losing all his material property.[5, 7]
His wanderings led him to Moravia, where he stayed in the town of Ungarisch Brod (Uherský Brod), but he found no rest there and had difficulty adapting to the new conditions.[5] When the political situation stabilized, the Taz returned to Poland and settled in Lviv, a city that had also been severely damaged but had begun a process of rehabilitation.[3, 5] In 1654 he was appointed rabbi of the city and head of the rabbinic court of Lviv, a position he held until the day of his death.[3, 5] In Lviv the Taz worked to rebuild the world of Torah and the communities that had been destroyed, serving as one of the heads of the "Council of Four Lands" and charting the halakhic and moral path for wounded Polish Jewry.[4]
The impact of the decrees is evident in his works, both in the theological tone of lament over the communities that were destroyed and in practical halakhic solutions to problems created in the wake of the war, such as questions of agunot (women unable to remarry) and the restoration of communal property.[12] The Taz saw his Torah work as a kind of "light out of darkness", an attempt to restore order and clarity to a world that had been destroyed around him.[4]
Methodology of Study and Ruling: Toil and Clarification
The Taz represents a scholarly school that places intellectual exertion at the center as a supreme religious value. In his view, the Torah is acquired only by one who "kills himself over it", a concept he interpreted not as bodily mortification but as total devotion to "pilpul" and to in-depth halakhic deliberation.[4] His Torah toil was not intended as a mere display of acuity but as the clarification of the pure truth out of the sea of disputes.[4]
The Struggle against "Two Torahs"
One of the central motives for writing the "Turei Zahav" was the Taz's feeling that the multiplicity of opinions and disputes in his generation might lead to a splitting of the Torah into "two Torahs".[4, 8] After the publication of the Shulchan Arukh of Rabbi Yosef Karo and the glosses of the Rema, many commentaries and rulings that contradicted one another began to appear, which created confusion among students and judges. The Taz sought to create a code that would clarify the words of the "Tur" and the "Shulchan Arukh", decide between the various opinions and establish the halakha precisely, in an accessible and authoritative manner.[4]
The choice of the name "Turei Zahav" reflects this mission: it is a play on words on the biblical expression "We will make you circlets of gold" (torei zahav na'aseh lakh) from the Song of Songs, but with a change of spelling that alludes to the "Tur", on which the Taz based the structure of his commentary.[4, 5, 8] In his eyes, the "Tur" is the solid foundation, and he came to overlay it with the "gold" of explanation and clarity.[5, 8]
The Esoteric Element: Divine Inspiration within Halakha
Although the works of the Taz appear to be a distinctly rational-halakhic work, there is broad agreement among the great figures of later generations, and especially in the Hasidic movement, that his writing was done with "divine inspiration" (ruach ha-kodesh).[4, 6] The Alter Rebbe, the author of the Tanya, testified that the Taz was granted the revelation of secrets of the Torah that found expression in the precision of his rulings.[4, 6]
This insight deepens the understanding of the figure of the Taz; he did not see textual analysis as a technical operation but as a vessel for drawing down the Divine Presence. His rulings, even when they seem difficult to understand with the tools of pure logic, are regarded as drawing on esoteric sources of hidden wisdom.[4] This connection between the revealed and the hidden also finds expression in the gematria of his name – "David" (14), which is the numerical value alluded to in the name of his work – and in traditions that tell how his halakhic decisions directly affected the metaphysical reality and brought about salvations.[4]
The Literary Work: Foundations of Ashkenazi Halakhic Ruling
The Taz left behind a written legacy that encompasses all layers of Jewish life. His principal work, "Turei Zahav", was printed in parts over some hundred years, but its importance was recognized immediately upon its appearance.[1, 3, 5]
Turei Zahav on the Shulchan Arukh
The work is divided according to the four parts of the Shulchan Arukh, with each part having a character and style suited to its subject:
Yoreh De'ah: The first part to be printed (Lublin, 1646). This is his most fundamental work, dealing with the laws of the forbidden and the permitted, ritual slaughter, treifot and forbidden foods.[1, 5] In this part the Taz excels in examining the sources of the law and in his ability to decide complicated disputes among the Rishonim.[13, 14]
Orach Chaim: Printed in the year 5452 (1692) in Dyhernfurth by Shabbetai Bass.[5, 7] In this part the commentary is sometimes called "Magen David", and together with the "Magen Avraham" they are called "Maginei Eretz" (Shields of the Land).[5, 8] Here the Taz focuses on the laws of daily life, prayer, Shabbat and festivals, with particular care for the customs of Ashkenaz and Poland.[7, 15]
Choshen Mishpat and Even ha-Ezer: These parts were printed later (1761 and 1754 respectively).[5] They deal with monetary law, civil law, marriage and divorce. His writing in these parts is marked by an attempt to create harmony between the Jewish legal system and the changing communal reality.[5, 16]
Divrei David
Beyond his halakhic work, the Taz composed the book "Divrei David", an in-depth supercommentary on Rashi's commentary on the Torah.[1, 3, 16] The work, first printed in 1689, reveals another side of the Taz's personality – the biblical exegete who seeks to reconcile the plain meaning of Scripture with Midrash and halakha.[3, 7] In "Divrei David" he displays linguistic and theological erudition, engaging with earlier commentators and defending Rashi's approach as the central commentary on the Torah.[16]
The Controversy with the Shach: A Clash of Giants
One of the most famous and influential chapters in the history of halakha is the scholarly confrontation between the Taz and Rabbi Shabbetai HaKohen (the Shach).[1, 4, 17] The two giants published their commentaries on "Yoreh De'ah" in the very same year (1646).[7] The Taz was then 60 years old, a veteran and established decisor, while the Shach was only 24, a young genius who sought to challenge earlier conventions.[4, 7]
The Shach wrote a critical work called "Nekudot ha-Kesef", in which he takes issue with the words of the Taz decisively, sometimes in sharp language.[4, 9, 18] The Taz did not remain silent and replied in a special preface printed at the end of the "Yoreh De'ah", called "Daf ha-Acharon", in which he answers the Shach's criticism and defends his approach.[9]
Despite the deep halakhic dispute, mutual respect and esteem prevailed between the two. It is told that when the Shach was forced to flee from pogroms, he came to Lviv and was a guest in the home of the Taz.[4] The two sat together in the sukkah in the midst of the festival, and according to legend, their joy was so great that the Divine Presence rested upon them as at the Rejoicing of the Water-Drawing (Simchat Beit ha-Sho'evah).[4]
Over the generations, the "Council of Four Lands" first decided to rule according to the Taz (1683), but in the following centuries the Shach was accepted as the decisive authority in most cases in the Jewry of Poland and Lithuania.[9] Nevertheless, the page layout of the Shulchan Arukh, in which the Taz and the Shach appear on either side of the central text, made them inseparable partners in the study of halakha, each of them illuminating a different facet of the topic.[3, 7]
Notable Halakhic Rulings: Innovation and Tradition
The rulings of the Taz are characterized by a combination of stringency in matters of holiness and leniency in places where the law permits it, in order to prevent great financial loss or harm to the public.[6, 8]
The Sanctity of the Synagogue and Living above It
One of the rulings most identified with the Taz is the prohibition against living above a synagogue.[8] The Taz based this on his personal experience in Krakow, but deepened its halakhic foundation by holding that the sanctity of the synagogue must be supreme, and that any profane use – such as eating, sleeping or other needs – on the floor above constitutes a disgrace to the place of prayer.[1, 8] This ruling changed the conception of the architecture of communal buildings in Ashkenazi Jewry.
Signs of Purity and Forbidden Foods
The Taz dealt extensively with the laws of treifot and the signs of birds. He engaged with the positions of the Rambam and the Geonim concerning the signs of a kosher bird, demanding maximal precision in signs such as the "extra toe" and the "peelable gizzard".[13] His ruling concerning hard cheese (such as cheese aged six months) is an example of his ability to define clear physical criteria for halakha: in his view, cheese that does not have special fat and sharpness does not require waiting six hours between eating it and meat; wiping and rinsing the mouth suffice.[9]
Tefillin and Mezuzah
The Taz introduced significant innovations in the laws of writing STaM (Torah scrolls, tefillin and mezuzot). He ruled on the space required between the passages in tefillin, combining the position of the Rambam with that of the Rosh and creating an "intermediate formula" of nine composite letters.[9] In the laws of mezuzah, the Taz dealt with the exact placement in complex doorways (such as a doorway leading to a courtyard with a separate entrance), determining that one follows the hinge of the door ("heker tzir"), a ruling widely quoted in modern books on mezuzah.[9]
The Taz and His Public Leadership in Time of Crisis
The Taz was not only a man of halakha in his study; he was called upon to lead the surviving remnant after the destruction of Tach ve-Tat. As head of the rabbinic court in Lviv and as a leader in the Council of Four Lands, he dealt with questions of rehabilitating families that had been shattered, settling the debts of communities that had been destroyed, and restoring spiritual security to the Jews of Poland.[4, 12]
The Sabbatean Crisis: Between Hope and Caution
In 1666, when Shabbetai Tzvi began to become known as the "Messiah", Polish Jewry was in desperate need of tidings of redemption.[5] The Taz, by then an old man of about 80, showed great interest in the movement. He sent his son Rabbi Yeshaya and his stepson Rabbi Aryeh Leib to Turkey to investigate the nature of Shabbetai Tzvi.[5, 8] The emissaries returned with a positive impression and even brought their father a letter and a white silk garment from the "Messiah".[5]
Nevertheless, the Taz was careful not to express sweeping public support. He remained "on the fence", following developments with caution.[8] After Shabbetai Tzvi's conversion to Islam, the moderate leadership of the Taz helped the Lviv community pass through the crisis without the social disintegration that other communities experienced.[7] His figure served as an anchor of stability within the stormy sea of false messianism.
A Legacy for the Generations: The Influence on the World of Halakha
The passing of the Taz on 26 Shevat 5427 (1667) marked the end of an era in Polish Jewry, but his works were only beginning their historical journey.[1, 3, 8] His standing as "the last of the Acharonim", whose ruling is final and binding, was quickly established.
The Taz in the Mirror of the Decisors of the Following Centuries
All the major decisors who arose after him regarded the Taz as an authority of the first rank:
The Pri Megadim (18th century): Rabbi Yosef Teomim wrote his monumental work on the Shulchan Arukh as a commentary on the Taz and the Shach, defending the position of the Taz in many places and explaining his words.[9, 20]
The Mishnah Berurah (19th century): Rabbi Yisrael Meir HaKohen (the Chofetz Chaim) bases most of his decisions in "Orach Chaim" on the words of the Taz, and presents his disputes with the "Magen Avraham" as the basis for modern halakhic discussion.[21, 22]
The Aruch ha-Shulchan: Rabbi Yechiel Michel Epstein treats the Taz as a pillar of Ashkenazi halakha and quotes him in almost every section.[9, 23]
A Symbol of Humility and Toil
The figure of the Taz became a symbol of "Torah out of poverty". Stories about the old, torn tallit in which he prayed for years, claiming that it would testify for him in the World to Come that he had never had an improper thought while wearing the tzitzit, rooted in the public mind his image as a pious and holy man.[4] Traditions telling how his body remained intact hundreds of years after his death added to the mythic dimension of his figure.[4]
The grave of the Taz in Lviv remained a focus of pilgrimage even in difficult times. Although the cemetery was desecrated by the Soviets and turned into a market, Jewish efforts to commemorate his burial place did not cease, and in 2014 a tombstone was erected there anew, serving as physical testimony to the continuity of his legacy.[2]
Summary: The Golden Pillar of the Shulchan Arukh
Rabbi David HaLevi Segal, the Taz, is not merely a commentator on the Shulchan Arukh; he is the senior partner in shaping the halakhic code as we know it today.[5, 7] His work combines the best of the tradition of Ashkenazi scholarship: analytical acuity that does not come at the expense of practical clarity, deep commitment to the tradition of the generations together with the courage to decide new questions, and a life of Torah toil that served as a spiritual response to physical destruction.[4]
His Torah teaching, drawing on the depths of the "Tur" and rising to divine inspiration, continues to illuminate the study halls.[4, 22] As his older brother testified of him, the name of Rabbi David HaLevi went forth in all lands and his work won worldwide recognition, as he established for the generations "rows of gold" that will never grow dim.[4, 7] His figure remains a model of spiritual leadership in time of crisis, of a decisor who seeks the absolute truth, and of a Torah scholar who sees in every difficulty and resolution a tool for repairing the world and bringing the redemption.[4, 8]
